Neonates of the Black salamander (Aneides flavipunctatus) emerge from the egg with a snout-vent length of 1.5 cm [Lb = 1.5 cm], a modest size that positions them among the smaller offspring of western plethodontids. This initial dimension, recorded from gravid females collected in Mendocino County and observed through to hatching in laboratory captivity, provides a baseline for examining subsequent growth trajectories. Like many direct-developing species within the genus, Aneides flavipunctatus bypasses the free-swimming larval stage entirely; the yolk-laden egg, deposited in a concealed terrestrial microhabitat such as a decaying log or a moss-covered rock crevice, sustains the developing embryo through to a fully formed, miniature adult. The efficiency of this endotrophic strategy is reflected in the consistent hatchling length observed across multiple clutches. Understanding the body size at emergence is crucial for evaluating early-life survival prospects, as smaller neonates may be more vulnerable to desiccation or predation in the damp but structurally complex environments these salamanders inhabit across their range in coastal California.

Reproductive investment in this species is well-documented under controlled thermal regimes. When females are maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a temperature that approximates the cool, humid conditions of their preferred microhabitats during the breeding season, they produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year]. Each clutch contains 28 eggs [N_R_i = 28 eggs], representing a considerable energetic commitment for a lungless salamander with a relatively slow metabolism. These parameters combine to yield a maximum annual reproductive output that is modest compared to many aquatic-breeding amphibians, but typical for a terrestrial direct-developer that must provision each egg with sufficient yolk for complete embryonic development. The extended incubation period at this temperature underscores the trade-off between developmental rate and the need for prolonged parental attendance, with the female often remaining coiled around the egg mass until hatching, presumably to defend against fungal infection and invertebrate predators.

Female Black salamanders attain a maximum snout-vent length of 8.7 cm [Li = 8.7 cm], a value that represents the upper asymptote of body size observed in field studies and museum collections across the species geographic range. This ultimate size is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 13.2 grams [Wwi = 13.2 grams], placing Aneides flavipunctatus among the larger members of its genus. The relationship between skeletal length and body mass is relatively isometric in this species, with the heaviest individuals typically being females carrying developing ova or fat reserves accumulated during the active foraging season. This asymptotic body size is likely constrained by the interplay of metabolic demand, the availability of invertebrate prey in the cool, moist forest floor habitats they occupy, and the biomechanical limits of lungless respiration. Comparisons with the related Desmognathus quadramaculatus, for which a size-corrected mass estimate was derived, suggest that the somatic investment in reaching this adult dimension is substantial.

Sexual maturation in Aneides flavipunctatus occurs upon attainment of a snout-vent length of 5.4 cm [Lp = 5.4 cm], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for reproduction. Individuals below this size are considered juveniles and are rarely observed engaging in courtship or amplexus in the wild. The transition to puberty appears to be more strongly correlated with body size than with chronological age, as growth rates can vary considerably with local thermal conditions, food availability, and habitat quality. In populations occupying warmer, drier sites at the southern edge of the species range, the time required to reach this pubertal length may be extended relative to those in cooler, more consistently moist coastal redwood forests. This size-based threshold likely ensures that only individuals with sufficient energy reserves and body condition can successfully allocate resources toward gamete production, thereby reducing the risk of reproductive failure during the energetically demanding breeding season.

Longevity records for the Black salamander, based on mark-recapture studies and captive observations at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 27 years [am = 27 years], an exceptional duration for a salamander of its body size and one that underscores the slow pace of its life history. This extended lifespan is characteristic of the genus Aneides, which includes some of the longest-lived terrestrial salamanders known, and is linked to their low metabolic rates, secretive habits, and occupation of relatively stable, predator-buffered microhabitats like deep rock fissures and the interior of large, decaying logs. Females, in particular, may invest many years in reaching sexual maturity and then reproduce only intermittently, with biennial or even triennial breeding cycles suspected in some populations. The trade-off between delayed maturity and high adult survival is a recurring theme in the life history of these salamanders, with the accumulation of reproductive opportunities over a long adult lifespan offsetting the low annual fecundity. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with older individuals maintaining body condition and breeding capability well into their third decade.
